RTX 5090 Power Connectors Are Melting, and Manufacturers Are Denying Warranty Claims

By Keith Mitchell Posted: October 6, 2026 11:49 AM EDT

I own an NVIDIA RTX 5090 (and no I didn’t spend more than my entire year’s mortgage costs), a graphics card that costs thousands of dollars, and lately I’ve found myself doing something I never thought I’d have to do: periodically pulling the side panel off my PC just to make sure the damned power connector isn’t melting.

That’s where we are with the RTX 5090 right now, and it’s starting to piss me off.

I’ve been building my own PCs for as long as I can remember. Sure, I destroyed a few CPUs along the way. Gotta love forgetting the heatsink on those old AMD Durons, because those things burned up really fast. But I’ve been doing a pretty damn good job ever since. Yet despite all those years of building PCs, I’ve never felt like I needed to worry this much about whether an expensive piece of hardware could damage itself simply because of the power connection being used.

What makes it worse is that PC hardware is more expensive than ever, especially at the high end. An RTX 5090 can cost several thousand dollars, and at the same time we’re seeing reports of melted power connectors, manufacturers fighting customers over RMAs, and warranty claims potentially being denied because someone used the native 12V-2×6 cable that came with their power supply instead of the adapter included with the graphics card.

Advertisement

That’s not exactly what you want to see when people are spending thousands of dollars on this stuff.

The biggest example right now is the RTX 5090 and the never-ending mess with its power connector. We’ve already been through this with the RTX 4090, and despite the newer 12V-2×6 design, we’re still seeing reports of RTX 5090 power connectors melting. There have even been reports involving RTX 5080 cards, so this isn’t something limited to just one model.

And these aren’t just random stories floating around social media. In one recent case, PNY reportedly denied an RTX 5090 warranty claim after the owner used the native 12V-2×6 cable supplied with an ASRock PG-1600G power supply instead of a PNY-approved cable or adapter. According to the report, the card wasn’t even overclocked, and the owner had actually reduced its power limit.

Then there was another case involving a $5,245 Digital Storm prebuilt with a PNY RTX 5090. The connectors reportedly melted after the PC was put into regular use, and both Digital Storm and PNY reportedly denied coverage for different reasons. PNY again pointed to the use of third-party PSU cables.

Advertisement

We’ve also seen an MSI RTX 5090 Gaming Trio OC suffer a melted connector while using Corsair’s own first-party 600W cable. That’s what makes this even more frustrating, because these aren’t all cases of people using questionable hardware or doing something obviously wrong. This one hit home because this is the same card that I have, just with a higher spec’d PSU.

We’re now at a point where someone can spend several thousand dollars on a graphics card, connect it to a modern ATX 3.1 power supply using the PSU manufacturer’s own native GPU cable, have the connector melt, and potentially be told they used the wrong cable. For anyone who builds PCs, that’s absolutely ridiculous. Mind you, we’re seeing RTX 5090s selling for more than $4,000 in some cases right now, which is just crazy (see the first image in this article).

And this one hit home for me because I own an RTX 5090. I’m not using the official cable that came with it, either. I’m using the proper cable from a $300 Corsair HX1200i power supply, and every time I use my PC, there’s still that little thought in my head hoping I don’t suddenly smell something burning. it’s always why every so often I pull the side off my case to check for any potential issues.

Now I’m at the point where I’m reaching out to the company that made my GPU and asking them bluntly, “If my GPU burns up because I’m not using the official cable that came with it, is it still covered under warranty?” I can’t believe that’s even a question I need to ask, but here we are. If you own an RTX 5090, I recommend doing the same thing and getting that answer in writing.

Advertisement

And if you’re thinking about getting an RTX 5090, heck, any NVIDIA graphics card that uses that dumb power connection, including the RTX 5080, you may also want to think about getting some kind of extra protection plan from wherever you buy it. Best Buy, Micro Center, whatever. Just something extra in case the manufacturer decides to give you a hard time later.

It’s crazy that I’m even saying that, because when you’re spending this kind of money, the manufacturer’s warranty should be enough. You shouldn’t have to buy extra protection because you’re worried someone is going to find a reason to deny your claim.

For years, one of the reasons to buy a newer power supply with a native 12VHPWR or 12V-2×6 cable was so you didn’t have to use the adapters that come with the GPU. PSU companies advertise these cables as a feature, and we’re supposed to trust that they’re designed to power these graphics cards properly. If NVIDIA or one of its board partners wants you to use only the cable or adapter that comes with the graphics card, then say that clearly. Put it on the box, put it in the warranty, and make sure nobody can miss it.

Don’t wait until someone’s multi-thousand-dollar graphics card melts and then tell them, “Well, you should have used our cable.” Because if I need to worry about which perfectly valid cable I’m allowed to plug into my GPU just to make sure my warranty is still good, then something has gone seriously wrong with PC hardware.

Advertisement

Meanwhile, NVIDIA is sitting in the background and, at least publicly, doesn’t seem to be saying much about any of this. In my view, they’re the company that should be stepping in, addressing the issue, and making it clear what owners are supposed to use and what should still be covered under warranty. After all, this whole mess centers around the power connection used on their GPUs, so they shouldn’t be leaving board partners, PSU companies, and customers to sort it out among themselves.

Maybe I should dig around my GPU boxes and just connect those damned original power cables, just in case.
